name: Mercado Roma
blurb: Three-floor food hall on Querétaro. Pricier than the city's actual mercados, but well-curated. Drinks at the rooftop are the move.
tips: Skip the crowded ground floor — head up
Open Tue–Sun, closed Mondays

name: Plaza Río de Janeiro
blurb: The David replica fountain. Roma Norte's photogenic centerpiece, ringed by cafés and the occasional jacaranda in May.
tips: Cucurucho coffee on the south edge
Wander Orizaba in either direction for the prettiest streets

name: Parque México
blurb: Condesa's social heart. Dogs, runners, an art-deco bandshell. Loop it once for orientation, then come back at sunset.
tips: Best at golden hour
Sunday mornings are full of families and Sunday newspapers

name: Licorería Limantour
blurb: World's-50-Best cocktail bar that actually lives up to the rep. Get there before 8 or accept a wait.
tips: Reserve online; walk-in is rough on weekends
Order the Margarita Al Pastor

name: Contramar
blurb: Lunch only, weekends booked weeks out. Tuna tostadas and grilled snapper. Most people's answer to 'one meal in CDMX.'
tips: Reserve a month ahead for weekends
Aim for 1:30 pm if walking in midweek

name: Zócalo
blurb: Plaza de la Constitución. Massive Mexican flag, surrounded by Catedral and Palacio Nacional. There's always something happening.
tips: Sunrise flag-raising is genuinely impressive
Climb to a rooftop bar (Gran Hotel CDMX) for the view
facts: One of the largest city squares in the world — about 240 m on a side, big enough to land a plane
Built directly over the sacred precinct of Tenochtitlan — Templo Mayor's foundation runs under the cathedral and Palacio Nacional
The flag in the center is 25 m wide and lowered every evening by a full military ceremony
Officially named Plaza de la Constitución — 'Zócalo' (literally 'pedestal') stuck because a monument's pedestal sat unused here for decades in the 19th century

name: Catedral Metropolitana
blurb: Four-hundred-year-old cathedral, sinking unevenly into the lakebed. Free entry, and the floor is noticeably tilted underfoot.
tips: Side chapels are quieter than the nave
Watch the floor — you can feel the slope
facts: Construction started in 1573 and didn't finish until 1813 — 240 years across three architectural styles
Built using stones from the Templo Mayor pyramid the Spanish destroyed — a deliberate symbolic erasure of the Aztec capital
It has been sinking unevenly for centuries — engineers spent the 1990s injecting concrete under the foundations to slow the tilt
The Altar of the Kings inside is one of the most ornate Baroque artworks in the Americas

name: Templo Mayor
blurb: Aztec ruins beside the cathedral, with an excellent attached museum. Half-hour minimum, two hours if you read everything.
tips: Combo with the cathedral — they're 100 m apart
Closed Mondays
facts: The site was lost for centuries — rediscovered in 1978 when electricity workers struck a stone disk of the goddess Coyolxauhqui
It was the spiritual heart of Tenochtitlan: a double pyramid honoring Huitzilopochtli (war/sun) and Tlaloc (rain)
Each Aztec ruler enlarged the pyramid, so the site has seven nested temples — like an architectural matryoshka
Spanish conquistadors deliberately demolished it in 1521 and built the cathedral over the holiest part of the precinct

name: Palacio de Bellas Artes
blurb: Art-deco/art-nouveau theater on the edge of Alameda Central. Murals by Rivera, Orozco, Siqueiros inside. Worth going in even without a show.
tips: Cross the street to Sears for the postcard view from the 8th-floor café
Closed Mondays
facts: The white Carrara marble exterior is so heavy the building has sunk about four meters since it was finished in 1934
Diego Rivera's 'Man at the Crossroads' inside is a recreated version of the mural Rockefeller had destroyed in New York for including Lenin
The stained-glass curtain in the theater was made by Tiffany Studios — one ton of opalescent glass, a depiction of the Valley of Mexico's volcanoes
Construction started in 1904 under Porfirio Díaz and was paused for 30 years by the Revolution

name: Torre Latinoamericana
blurb: 1956 skyscraper, observation deck on 44. Best panorama of the city by far on a clear day — and an engineering marvel for surviving 1985.
tips: Go on a clear morning before the smog rises
The combo museum ticket is barely worth it
facts: When it opened in 1956 it was the tallest building in Latin America at 182 m
It is the world's first skyscraper built on highly seismic land — engineer Leonardo Zeevaert designed deep friction piles that let the tower 'float' on the soft lakebed
Survived the 1985 earthquake (8.1 magnitude) without a crack while older, lower buildings nearby collapsed
Survived a 2017 earthquake (7.1) the same way — its design is still studied in seismic engineering

name: Palacio Nacional
blurb: Diego Rivera's monumental staircase murals — the visual history of Mexico, panel by panel. Free with ID.
tips: Bring your passport — they actually check
Often closed weekends — go midweek
facts: Built on the site of Moctezuma II's palace — Hernán Cortés used the original stones to construct his own residence here in 1521
Diego Rivera painted the staircase murals between 1929 and 1935 — they show Mexican history from pre-Hispanic times through the Revolution
The 'Bell of Dolores,' which Father Hidalgo rang in 1810 to start the War of Independence, hangs over the central balcony
Every September 15 the President rings that bell at 11 pm to begin the 'Grito de Independencia' ceremony

name: Casa de los Azulejos
blurb: 16th-century palace covered in blue-and-white Talavera tiles. Houses a Sanborns now — walk in for the courtyard and the Orozco mural over the back staircase.
tips: Free to enter — no ticket needed for the courtyard
Don't miss the José Clemente Orozco mural up the back stairs
Coffee or breakfast inside is touristy but the room is worth it
facts: Legend has it the heir added the tiles in the 18th century to spite his father, who told him he'd 'never build a house of tiles'
Belonged for centuries to the Counts of the Valle de Orizaba, one of New Spain's wealthiest families
The Sanborns chain has occupied it since 1919 — it functions as both a national monument and a fast-food coffee shop

name: Plaza de Santo Domingo
blurb: The second great plaza of Centro, three blocks north of the Zócalo. Lined with arcades where 'evangelistas' (typists for hire) have sat since the 19th century.
tips: Best in the morning when the typists set up their tables
Santo Domingo church and the old Inquisition palace face each other across the square
Hostería de Santo Domingo for lunch is a block away
facts: A gathering place since Aztec times — the original Templo Mayor sacred precinct extended this far north
Public scribes still type letters and fill out forms on typewriters under these arcades — a profession centuries old
The former Palace of the Inquisition on the east side now houses the Mexican medical history museum

name: Antiguo Colegio de San Ildefonso
blurb: Where Mexican muralism was born. Rivera, Orozco, and Siqueiros painted their first major murals on these courtyard walls in the 1920s. Now a museum with rotating exhibits.
tips: Closed Mondays
Combine with Templo Mayor — they're a 5-minute walk apart
The murals on the open courtyard walls are visible from the entry hall
facts: Diego Rivera's 'La Creación' (1922) here was his first mural — and the first major mural of the modern Mexican movement
It was a Jesuit school from 1588 until the Jesuits were expelled from New Spain in 1767
José Vasconcelos (yes, the library's namesake) commissioned the murals as Education Minister to literally re-paint Mexico's identity

name: Museo Nacional de Arte (MUNAL)
blurb: Mexico's flagship museum of Mexican art from the 16th century to the mid-20th. Beaux-Arts palace, broad collection, far less crowded than Antropología.
tips: Closed Mondays
The José María Velasco landscapes alone are worth the visit
Free Sundays — but you trade quiet for the crowd
facts: Houses the largest collection of Mexican paintings in the country
The bronze equestrian statue of King Carlos IV out front — known as 'El Caballito' — is one of the largest cast-bronze statues in the world
The building was originally the Ministry of Communications, finished in 1911 just months before the Revolution overthrew its patrons

name: Museo Mural Diego Rivera
blurb: A single-mural museum, built around Rivera's 'Sueño de una Tarde Dominical en la Alameda Central.' The mural was rescued after the 1985 earthquake destroyed its original hotel.
tips: Small museum — an hour is plenty
Closed Mondays
Right at the west end of Alameda — easy combo with a stroll
facts: The mural depicts Rivera himself as a child, holding hands with La Catrina — the iconic skeleton dame invented by José Guadalupe Posada
Originally painted for the Hotel del Prado in 1947 — the hotel's main entrance was built around the mural
When the 1985 earthquake collapsed the hotel, the 15 m mural was carefully cut from the wall and moved here in one piece

name: Plaza Garibaldi
blurb: The mariachi plaza. Bands in full charro suits stand around waiting to be hired by the song. Loudest after dark — go with company and stay aware.
tips: Negotiate per song before they play — 100–200 pesos is standard
Museo del Tequila y el Mezcal (MUTEM) is right on the plaza
Don't wander north — Tepito's edge is one block away
Best with a few friends; not a solo-after-dark stop
facts: Mariachi bands have gathered here for hire since the 1920s — it's a working musicians' market, not a tourist show
The plaza was overhauled in 2010 to feel safer; it works at early evening, less so very late
Salón Tenampa, on the north edge, has poured tequila since 1925 and is where many mariachi standards were first popularized

name: Museo de la Ciudad de México
blurb: A 17th-century palace south of the Zócalo, telling the city's story. Smaller and quieter than MUNAL, with a serene courtyard.
tips: Free entry
Closed Mondays
Spot the Aztec serpent's head built into the corner of the building — recycled from a pre-Hispanic temple
facts: The corner stone is a carved feathered-serpent head from an Aztec temple — colonial builders just incorporated it into the palace foundation
Belonged to the Counts of Santiago de Calimaya for centuries
The painter Joaquín Clausell turned an upstairs room into his personal studio — every wall is covered in his sketches

name: Café de Tacuba
blurb: Open since 1912 in a former 17th-century convent. Classical Mexican comfort food — chiles en nogada, mole, enchiladas — under tile murals and chandeliers.
tips: Get a table in the main hall, not the side room
Order chiles en nogada when in season (Aug–Sept)
It's touristy now — go for the room and the history
facts: The rock band Café Tacvba named themselves after this restaurant — they used to eat here as students
The Talavera tile murals depict the supposed invention of mole by a 17th-century nun in Puebla
It still hosts a small estudiantina — a strolling string band in colonial dress — most evenings

name: El Cardenal
blurb: Among the best traditional Mexican breakfasts in the city. Hot chocolate with sweet bread, fresh ricotta, and the thickest tamales you'll meet. There's a quieter Hilton location across the street.
tips: Breakfast and lunch only — go before 11 am to skip the queue
Order the chocolate caliente with concha (sweet bread)
Closed late afternoons

name: Azul Histórico
blurb: Ricardo Muñoz Zurita's love letter to Mexican regional cooking, served in the leafy courtyard of a 17th-century palace. Reservations strongly recommended.
tips: Sit in the courtyard if it's not raining
Reserve online — walk-in lunches are often turned away
The 'manchamanteles' mole and chiles en nogada (in season) are the signatures

name: Limosneros
blurb: Modern Mexican with serious technique — pre-Hispanic ingredients, careful platings, and an excellent mezcal list. Smaller, quieter, and more chef-driven than its big-name neighbors.
tips: Reserve, especially weekends
Lean on the mezcal flight
The grasshopper guacamole is genuinely good if you're brave

name: Hostería de Santo Domingo
blurb: Open continuously since 1860. The oldest restaurant in Mexico City. Famous for chiles en nogada year-round (rare) and a stubbornly old-school atmosphere.
tips: Year-round chiles en nogada — they make their own walnut sauce daily
Lunch is the move; dinner crowd is thinner
Cash is still the path of least friction here
facts: The oldest continuously operating restaurant in Mexico City — founded in 1860
Famous for serving chiles en nogada year-round; most places only offer them for two months in late summer
The painted dining room hasn't really changed since the early 20th century — by design

name: Bar La Ópera
blurb: An 1895 cantina with carved mahogany, mirrored ceilings, and a bullet hole said to be from Pancho Villa. The atmosphere is the order; the food is honest.
tips: Look up — staff will point out the Villa bullet hole in the ceiling
Tequila and cantina classics, not cocktails
Closed Sundays
facts: Pancho Villa is said to have ridden in on horseback in 1910 and fired a shot into the ceiling — the hole is still pointed out
Originally a French-style café opened in 1876, converted to a cantina in 1895
The carved bar and mirrored ceilings were imported from New Orleans

name: Balcón del Zócalo
blurb: Rooftop terrace of the Zócalo Central hotel, perched directly over the plaza with the Cathedral as backdrop. Drinks beat the food — but the view is the point.
tips: Reserve a sunset table — they fill fast on clear evenings
Mezcal cocktails are the move
Lunch is generally easier than dinner for walk-ins

name: Terraza del Gran Hotel CDMX
blurb: Rooftop with the most direct, head-on view of the Zócalo flag. The hotel lobby's stained-glass Tiffany ceiling alone is worth a quick detour even if you skip the bar.
tips: Walk through the lobby on the way up to see the Tiffany ceiling
A coffee or single drink is enough — the food is overpriced
Best at dawn or dusk when the flag is being raised or lowered
facts: The lobby's stained-glass ceiling was designed in 1908 — a contemporary of Paris's Galeries Lafayette dome
The building was originally the Centro Mercantil department store before becoming a hotel
Daniel Craig's James Bond walks through this lobby in the opening sequence of 'Spectre' (2015)

name: El Mayor
blurb: Rooftop café-bar inside the Porrúa bookstore, looking straight down into Templo Mayor's excavation pit. The unsung best view in Centro.
tips: Skip the entrée menu — it's a bookshop's café upstairs
Coffee, beer, and aerial photos of the ruins
Closed Mondays when Templo Mayor closes

name: Biblioteca Vasconcelos
blurb: The 'megabiblioteca.' A 250-meter-long suspended-shelf library that looks like Borges and Escher built it together. Floating bookcases, a full whale skeleton, and a botanical garden out back.
tips: Free entry — bring ID, leave bags at the lockers near the entrance
Closed Mondays — open 8:30 am to 7:30 pm other days
Walk all the way to the back — most people stop halfway and miss Gabriel Orozco's whale (Mátrix Móvil)
The botanical garden behind the library is a quiet payoff after the architecture
Photographs allowed without flash — early morning is the cleanest light
facts: Inaugurated in 2006, designed by Alberto Kalach — the multi-story shelves appear to float because the structure hangs from the roof, not the floor
Holds nearly 600,000 volumes across seven cantilevered levels stacked the length of two football fields
The suspended grey whale skeleton in the central nave is by Gabriel Orozco — titled 'Mátrix Móvil,' it was assembled from a real whale that washed up in Baja California
Named for José Vasconcelos, the Education Minister who launched Mexico's public library system in the 1920s and commissioned the muralist movement
Closed within a year of opening due to construction defects — it reopened in 2008 after extensive repairs
The botanical garden behind the building has 60,000 plants representing every ecoregion of Mexico

name: Monumento a la Revolución
blurb: Massive copper-domed art-deco arch built from the abandoned skeleton of a never-finished Porfirian palace. Ride the glass elevator inside the dome for a 360° view.
tips: Take the elevator to the dome (small fee) for the view
Closed Mondays for the elevator and museum
Walkable from Vasconcelos in 15–20 minutes south
The plaza around it has dancing fountains in the evening
facts: Originally meant to be the Federal Legislative Palace under Porfirio Díaz — construction began in 1910 and stopped when the Revolution broke out months later
Architect Carlos Obregón Santacilia salvaged the steel skeleton in 1933 and rebuilt it as a monument to the very revolution that killed the original project
Pancho Villa, Madero, Carranza, and Plutarco Elías Calles are entombed in the four corner pillars
At 67 m, it is one of the tallest triumphal arches in the world

name: Tianguis Cultural del Chopo
blurb: Saturday-only alternative-culture street market — the heart of Mexico City's punk, goth, metal, and underground scene since 1980. Vinyl, band shirts, zines, leather jackets.
tips: Saturdays only, roughly 11 am to 5 pm
Walking distance from Biblioteca Vasconcelos — combine them
Cash only at most stalls
Subcultures are friendlier than they look — go in respectful and curious
facts: Running every Saturday since 1980 — Mexico City's longest-continuing music subculture market
It originated as a tianguis around the Museo del Chopo (then a science museum) and never left the name
It's where countless Mexican rock and punk bands first sold demo tapes and self-released records

name: Museo Universitario del Chopo
blurb: Iron-and-glass art-nouveau pavilion (originally imported from Germany in the 1900s). Now a UNAM contemporary-art space — film, performance, queer and counter-cultural programming.
tips: Free or very cheap entry depending on the show
Closed Mondays
Easy cultural pairing with Vasconcelos and the Saturday tianguis
facts: The iron-and-glass structure was prefabricated in Düsseldorf in 1902 and shipped to Mexico in pieces
It opened in 1910 as Mexico City's first natural-history museum — dinosaur skeletons stayed for 50 years
Since 1975 it has been a UNAM cultural center — early supporter of queer, punk, and counter-cultural art before the mainstream caught up

name: Museo Nacional de Antropología
blurb: The big one. Aztec, Maya, Olmec, Zapotec, Teotihuacano. Allow at least three hours; you'll still leave wanting more.
tips: Start with Sala Mexica (Aztec) on the ground floor
Go on a weekday morning
Closed Mondays
facts: The central courtyard's giant umbrella fountain — 'El Paraguas' — is held up by a single 28 m column carved with pre-Hispanic motifs
Designed by Pedro Ramírez Vázquez and opened in 1964 — the architecture is considered one of the great works of 20th-century Mexican modernism
Houses the original Sun Stone (often miscalled the Aztec Calendar) and the colossal Olmec heads — both anchors of Mexican identity

name: Castillo de Chapultepec
blurb: Hilltop castle, former imperial residence under Maximilian. Sweeping view down Reforma. The walk up is steep but short.
tips: Closed Mondays
Combine with Antropología — a 15-minute walk apart through the park
facts: The only royal castle in the Americas to have housed actual European sovereigns — Emperor Maximilian and Empress Carlota lived here in the 1860s
Maximilian commissioned the broad avenue down the hill (now Paseo de la Reforma) so Carlota could see her palace from the city
It served as Mexico's presidential residence until 1939, when President Cárdenas turned it into the National History Museum

name: Museo Soumaya
blurb: The mirrored Slim-funded museum at Plaza Carso. Free. The collection is uneven; the building is the attraction. The Rodin floor punches above the rest.
tips: Go for the architecture and the Rodins
Uber there — Polanco-adjacent, not really walkable from Roma

name: Casa Azul (Frida Kahlo)
blurb: Frida Kahlo's house. The single most-booked museum in CDMX. Buy tickets online a week+ in advance — they sell out daily.
tips: Buy tickets online ahead — do not show up hoping
Closed Mondays
Pair with lunch on the Coyoacán plaza

name: Jardín Centenario / Plaza Hidalgo
blurb: The town-square heart of Coyoacán. Mariachis on weekends, churros in the corner, cobblestones throughout.
tips: The coyote fountain is the natural meeting point
Mercado de Coyoacán is two blocks east — get tostadas

name: Bazaar Sábado
blurb: Saturdays only. Plaza San Jacinto fills with crafts and art vendors — best craft shopping in the country if you're shopping at all.
tips: Go before noon to dodge the worst of the crowd
Carry cash — most stalls don't take cards
Saturdays only — don't show up any other day

name: Xochimilco Trajineras
blurb: Painted-boat tours of the canals. Touristy in the best sense — locals do this too. Bring food, music, and someone to argue with.
tips: Start at Embarcadero Cuemanco or Nuevo Nativitas, not Fernando Celada
Negotiate hourly, agree on price before boarding
Floating mariachis cost extra per song — fix that price too
